% Vietnamese needs the T5 font encoding (vntex, in TeX Live). T5 is a superset of the
% T1 repertoire for Latin text, so it is listed last and becomes the default; T1 stays
% available for the odd glyph. `times` maps rm/sf/tt to ptm/phv/pcr, all of which vntex
% provides in T5 (t5ptm.fd, t5phv.fd, t5pcr.fd). inconsolata (zi4) has no T5 variant and
% is therefore NOT loaded. T5 also defines the accent macros \h (hook above) and \horn,
% which figures/fig1_tokens.tex uses to draw isolated combining marks.
\usepackage[T1,T5]{fontenc}

\begin{abstract}
Written Vietnamese marks each syllable's onset, rime and tone, yet subword tokenizers split syllables without regard to this structure. Can large language models manipulate units they never receive as tokens? We introduce \noilai{}, a benchmark built on \vi{nói lái}, a Vietnamese wordplay that swaps rimes, onsets or tones between syllables. A rule engine encoding Vietnamese spelling generates \placeholder{10,000} automatically scored items for transformation, decoding and validity judgment, alongside attested folk and literary examples, with a probability sample judged by native speakers (\placeholder{$\alpha$, generator precision}). Across \placeholder{21} models, \placeholder{\hyp{1}: whether accuracy tracks the alignment of token boundaries with onset and rime beyond token count; best model vs.\ humans}. We then intervene on tokenization with the characters' meaning held fixed, re-encoding text between precomposed and combining diacritics and between tone-mark placement conventions, and estimate within-item causal effects on \noilai{} and on Vietnamese XCOPA (\placeholder{\hyp{3}, \hyp{4}}). Probes and activation patching in Gemma~3 1B and 4B \placeholder{\hyp{5}: where tone becomes decodable and whether it is used}. Hypotheses are pre-registered before any test-split run. We release the generator, syllable parser and re-encoding toolkit (\anonurl).
\end{abstract}
